content: Data structures are specialized formats for organizing, storing, and accessing data efficiently. Different structures offer varying performance characteristics for common operations like insertion, deletion, search, and traversal. Arrays store elements in contiguous memory locations, providing O(1) constant-time access to elements by index but requiring O(n) time for insertions or deletions that shift elements. Linked lists consist of nodes containing data and references to the next node, offering O(1) insertion and deletion at known positions but O(n) search time since nodes must be traversed sequentially. Stacks follow Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) ordering, supporting push (add) and pop (remove) operations at one end, useful for function calls, expression evaluation, and backtracking algorithms. Queues implement First-In-First-Out (FIFO) ordering, with elements added at one end and removed from the other, commonly used in scheduling and breadth-first searches. Trees organize data hierarchically with parent-child relationships; binary search trees maintain ordered data for O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion in balanced cases. Hash tables map keys to values using hash functions, providing average-case O(1) operations but requiring collision resolution strategies when different keys hash to the same location. Graphs represent entities (vertices) and relationships (edges) between them, supporting complex network modeling. Heaps maintain partial ordering, efficiently finding minimum or maximum values, and supporting priority queues. The choice of data structure significantly impacts program performance and should be based on the specific operations most frequently performed, expected data size, memory constraints, and implementation complexity.

scenario.title: Locker System Designer
scenario.content: Students design and implement virtual school storage systems using different data structures. The simulation represents data management challenges through a school metaphor: arrays as numbered lockers in rows, linked lists as chained lockers with directions to the next locker, hash tables as locker assignments based on student IDs, trees as hierarchical club storage systems, and graphs as social networks tracking borrowed items. Students can implement and test different organization schemes, observing in real-time how each structure handles operations like adding new students, finding specific items, or removing graduated students. The system automatically measures and displays performance metrics like access time, memory usage, and operation counts. Interactive scenarios challenge students to select optimal data structures for different school situations with specific constraints and usage patterns. Advanced features allow students to implement hybrid systems combining multiple structures, demonstrating real-world software design principles.

hypothesis.description: Students will compare data structure performance by analyzing operation time complexity in different scenarios. They will predict how structure choice affects program efficiency for specific usage patterns, and implement appropriate data structures for various algorithmic requirements.
